entry: Process of generating moving images digitally, usually in 3D. Computer animation is a digital successor to stop motion and [[Traditional animation|traditional animation]]. Instead of a physical model or drawing, an artist manipulates a digital equivalent frame by frame, which allows one graphic artist to produce content without actors, sets or props. Each image is replaced by a slightly advanced one, usually at 24, 25 or 30 frames per second, the same technique by which television and motion pictures create movement. Images should appear at around 12 frames per second or faster to trick the visual system into seeing smooth motion, and realistic imagery demands higher frame rates. In 3D work, animators pose rigged models at keyframes, and interpolation automates the inbetweening between them. The broader term computer-generated imagery (CGI) also covers still images.

Conceptual design and operational structure of a computer system. It is often a general description that ignores precise implementation details, and it describes how component parts are organized and interact to execute programs efficiently. The discipline covers the instruction set architecture (ISA), which defines the machine code a processor reads along with word size, memory addressing modes, registers and data types; microarchitecture, also called computer organization, which describes how a processor implements the ISA; and systems design, which includes other components such as direct memory access and virtualization. It weighs tradeoffs among performance, cost, power, reliability and security. The term "architecture" in this sense is traced to 1959 work at IBM on the Stretch supercomputer. The von Neumann architecture, outlined in John von Neumann's 1945 report, is the foundational model for most computer architectures.

Named collection of data treated as a unit by the system that manages it, called a [[File system|file system]]. Files may store a written message, document, spreadsheet, image, video or program, and some store several data types at once. Programs let a person open, read, change, save and close a file, which can be reopened, modified and copied an arbitrary number of times. On most modern operating systems, files are organized as one-dimensional arrays of bytes, and a file's format is defined by its content. A file manager lets users move, create, delete and rename files and directories, also called folders. Files can be transferred between computers and mobile devices by removable media, networks or the [[Internet|Internet]].

Field of computer science concerned with generating and manipulating images and art. Computer graphics is a core technology in digital photography, film, [[Video game|video games]], digital art and the displays of most devices. The phrase was coined in 1960 by Verne Hudson and William Fetter of Boeing. Computer-generated imagery is commonly divided into two-dimensional (2D), three-dimensional (3D) and animated graphics, and 3D graphics have become more common as technology has improved. Ivan Sutherland's *Sketchpad* (1963) introduced interactive, constraint-based drawing. Applications include entertainment, engineering design through CAD systems, medical imaging and scientific visualization. Modern work includes real-time ray tracing and GPU acceleration.

Physical components of a computer. Hardware includes the [[Central processing unit|central processing unit]] (CPU), [[Random-access memory|random-access memory]] (RAM), motherboard, data storage, graphics card, sound card and computer case, as well as external devices such as a monitor, mouse, keyboard and speakers. Software is a set of written instructions that hardware can store and run, and hardware is typically directed by software to execute commands. Some of the earliest devices date to the 17th century: [[Blaise Pascal]] designed a gear-based device that could add and subtract in 1642. [[Charles Babbage]] designed a general-purpose computer in the 19th century that was never built. In 1945 [[John von Neumann]] devised the von Neumann architecture, which stored programs and data in one memory and has served as the template for most modern computers.

Input device modeled on the [[Typewriter|typewriter]] keyboard, with keys that act as mechanical levers or electronic switches. Teleprinter-style keyboards have been the main input method for computers since the 1970s, supplemented by the [[Computer mouse|mouse]] since the 1980s and the touchscreen since the 2000s. Most keys produce a symbol, while others, such as the escape key, prompt the computer to execute system commands. The software interprets key presses, since the scan code tells the computer only which physical key was pressed or released. Most full-size keyboards use one of three mechanical layouts, ISO, ANSI or JIS. The QWERTY layout was patented in 1878 by Christopher Latham Sholes. Keyboards connect by USB, Bluetooth or wireless protocols, and mobile devices use virtual keyboards on their touchscreens.

Output device that displays information in pictorial or textual form. A monitor comprises a visual display, support electronics, a power supply, housing, electrical connectors and external controls. Modern monitors typically use an LCD with LED backlight, which replaced CCFL backlighting by the 2010s. Before the mid-2000s most monitors used a [[Cathode ray tube|cathode ray tube]] (CRT). Monitors connect to their host computer via [[DisplayPort|DisplayPort]], [[HDMI|HDMI]], [[USB-C|USB-C]], DVI or VGA. Since 2010 the typical display aspect ratio of both televisions and monitors has changed from 4:3 to 16:9. Most monitors lack integrated speakers or TV tuners. Monitors were formerly called visual display units (VDU), a term that mostly fell out of use by the 1990s.

Hand-held pointing device that controls a cursor on a display. A mouse detects two-dimensional motion relative to a surface and translates it into cursor movement, allowing smooth control of a graphical user interface. Most mice have one or more buttons for selecting menu items, and many add scroll wheels or touch surfaces. Early mice used two wheels and later a rolling ball, while most modern mice use optical detection with no moving parts. The first public demonstration was given by [[Douglas Engelbart]] in 1968 as part of The Mother of All Demos, and his design was patented in 1970. Xerox commercialized the mouse with the 8010 Star workstation in 1981, and Apple's Macintosh in 1984 popularized it for consumer use. Many modern mice are cordless and use short-range radio.

Group of communicating computers and peripherals, called hosts, that exchange data via communication protocols. Hosts are identified by network addresses and may also have hostnames. The physical medium may be copper cable, [[Optical fiber|optical fiber]] or radio, and the arrangement of hosts and hardware is called the network topology. In 1940 George Stibitz of Bell Labs connected a teletype at Dartmouth to a computing machine in New York, the first real-time remote use of a computing machine. Paul Baran and Donald Davies independently invented packet switching in the 1960s. [[ARPANET|ARPANET]] launched in 1969 as the first operational packet-switched network, and the Internet later became the largest wide area network, using the TCP/IP suite. Networks support the [[World Wide Web|World Wide Web]], email, printers and storage servers.

Sequence of instructions in a [[Programming language|programming language]] for a computer to execute. A program is one component of software, along with documentation and other intangible parts. In human-readable form it is called source code, which a [[Compiler|compiler]] translates into machine instructions as an executable file, or which an interpreter runs directly, more slowly. The operating system loads an executable into memory and starts a process, and the central processing unit fetches, decodes and executes each machine instruction. In 1843 [[Ada Lovelace]] published notes on [[Charles Babbage]]'s Analytical Engine that included a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers, which some historians regard as the first computer program. The [[ENIAC]] was built between July 1943 and fall 1945, and programming it took up to two months.

Process of writing sequences of instructions, called programs, that computers can follow. It typically involves designing and implementing [[Algorithm|algorithms]] in one or more [[Programming language|programming languages]]. Proficient programming usually requires knowledge of the application domain, programming languages, code libraries and formal logic. Related tasks include analyzing requirements, testing, debugging and maintaining build systems. The broader process is often called software development, and sometimes [[Software engineering|software engineering]]. Major paradigms include imperative (as in [[C (programming language)|C]] and [[Java (programming language)|Java]]), functional (as in Haskell and Scala), logical (as in Prolog) and object-oriented (as in [[C++|C++]] and [[Python (programming language)|Python]]). In the United States about 121,200 professionals were employed in programming as of 2024, with a median annual wage of $98,670 in May 2024.

Subdiscipline of information security concerned with protecting computer software, systems and networks. Also called cybersecurity, it addresses threats that can lead to unauthorized disclosure of information, theft or damage to hardware, software or data, and disruption of the services they provide. Reliance on computers, the Internet and smart devices such as [[Smartphone|smartphones]] has made security a critical concern. Estimates of global information security spending in 2026 range from US$244 billion to US$308 billion. A vulnerability is a flaw that compromises security, and an exploitable vulnerability is one for which a working exploit exists. Threats include [[Malware|malware]], [[Phishing|phishing]] and ransomware. In April 2023 a United Kingdom government report found that 32% of businesses and 24% of charities overall recalled a breach or attack in the previous 12 months, and small and midsize businesses have become increasingly vulnerable.

Running of a mathematical model on a computer to represent the behavior or outcome of a real-world or physical system. A model consists of the equations that capture a system's behavior, while the simulation is the running of a program that solves them, often approximately. Computer simulations are used in [[Physics|physics]], astrophysics, climatology, chemistry and biology, and in economics, psychology, social science, health care and engineering. Large-scale simulation first appeared in the [[Manhattan Project|Manhattan Project]] during World War II, when a [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo algorithm]] modeled nuclear detonation. In 1997 a simulated desert battle modeled 66,239 tanks, trucks and other vehicles around Kuwait, using multiple supercomputers. Other examples include a 2.64-million-atom model of the ribosome in 2005 and a complete simulation of the life cycle of *Mycoplasma genitalium* in 2012.

Self-replicating [[Malware|malware]] program that spreads across computer networks. A worm copies itself to other computers, often by exploiting security failures, and each infected machine becomes a host that scans for new targets, so infection grows rapidly. Unlike viruses, worms almost always harm networks, even if only by consuming bandwidth. The first was a self-replicating version of Creeper, created in 1971 by Ray Tomlinson and Bob Thomas at BBN to spread across the [[ARPANET|ARPANET]]. The Morris worm of 1988 disrupted many of the computers then connected to the Internet.

Goal-oriented activity that requires, benefits from or creates computing machinery. Computing includes the study of algorithmic processes and the development of hardware and software. Major disciplines include [[Computer science|computer science]], computer engineering, [[Software engineering|software engineering]], data science and information technology. The term was once synonymous with counting and calculating. The earliest known computing tool is the [[Abacus|abacus]], thought to have been invented in Babylon c. 2700 to 2300 BC. [[Claude Shannon]]'s 1938 paper introduced the use of electronics for Boolean algebraic operations. Researchers at Bell Labs built the first working [[Transistor|transistor]] in 1947, and the MOSFET followed in 1960, enabling dense [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuits]] and the microcomputer revolution.

Port city (pop., 2025: 3,407,327), capital and largest city of [[Guinea|Guinea]]. Conakry was first settled on the small Tombo Island and later spread to the Kaloum Peninsula. It was founded after Britain ceded the island to France in 1887, and it became the capital of French Guinea in 1904. A railway to Kankan opened the interior for the export of groundnuts, and the deepwater port handles exports of bauxite. The city's population grew from 50,000 in 1958 to 600,000 in 1980 and to more than 3.4 million later. Conakry has a tropical monsoon climate, with a dry season dominated by the harmattan wind from December to April and a wet season in which rainfall averages more than 1,100 mm (43 in) in both July and August.

American television host, comedian and writer. O'Brien wrote for [[Saturday Night Live|Saturday Night Live]] and [[The Simpsons|The Simpsons]] before hosting *Late Night with Conan O'Brien* on [[NBC|NBC]] from 1993 to 2009, making him the longest-serving host of that franchise. He then hosted *The Tonight Show with Conan O'Brien* for seven months in 2009–2010 and *Conan* on TBS until 2021. He later hosted the podcast *Conan O'Brien Needs a Friend* and received the 2025 Mark Twain Prize for American Humor.

Fundamental unit of cognition that classifies entities and encodes shared features. Concepts make it possible to form and combine ideas, draw [[Inference|inferences]] and refer to external objects. They act as the meanings of words and play a central role in cognitive processes including [[Perception|perception]], [[Memory|memory]] and reasoning. The classical theory holds that concepts are definitions with fixed rules for the entities they apply to. Prototype theory holds that membership depends on similarity to a prototype, and exemplar theory holds that similarity derives from memories of concrete instances. Philosophers debate whether concepts are mental representations or abstract objects. Suggested mechanisms of concept learning include associative learning and hypothesis testing, while nativism and empiricism differ on whether concepts are inborn. Concepts are relevant to psychology, philosophy and linguistics.

Art movement in which the concept behind a work takes priority over its material form. Also called conceptualism, it may be realized by anyone following a set of written instructions. Sol LeWitt defined it: "In conceptual art the idea or concept is the most important aspect of the work." [[Marcel Duchamp|Marcel Duchamp]]'s readymades are regarded as precursors, such as *Fountain* (1917), a standard urinal presented as art. Joseph Kosuth's 1969 essay "Art after Philosophy" argued that art exists conceptually, and the Art & Language collective, founded in 1968, published the journal *Art-Language*. In the United Kingdom, popular usage came to denote all [[Contemporary art|contemporary art]] that does not practice painting and sculpture. Critics argue that the movement conflates philosophy or rhetoric with art and diminishes the value of skill, while supporters credit it with broadening artistic discourse.

Live performance of music in front of an audience. A concert may be carried by a single musician, when it is often called a recital, or by an ensemble such as an [[Orchestra|orchestra]], [[Choir|choir]] or band. Concerts take place in settings from private houses and nightclubs to concert halls, arenas, stadiums, amphitheaters and parks. Before recorded music, concerts were the main opportunity to hear musicians play. The first known concert charging admission took place in 1672 at the London home of violinist John Banister. In 1678 Thomas Britton began weekly concerts in Clerkenwell, sold by yearly subscription at 10 shillings a year. In France, Anne Danican Philidor organized the Concerts Spirituels, held on religious holidays when the opera was closed. In the 1960s rock concerts became associated with countercultural fashion and attitudes.

Musical composition for one or more soloists accompanied by an orchestra or other ensemble. The typical three-movement structure, with a slow movement preceded and followed by fast ones, became standard in the early 18th century. The genre originated in vocal music in the late 16th century, and its instrumental form appeared about a century later. [[Antonio Vivaldi]] and other Venetian composers wrote hundreds of violin concertos. The first keyboard concertos were written by [[George Frideric Handel|George Frideric Handel]] and [[Johann Sebastian Bach|Johann Sebastian Bach]]. In the Classical era [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart|Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]] composed 27 piano concertos, and [[Ludwig van Beethoven|Ludwig van Beethoven]] treated the orchestra as an equal partner to the soloist. [[Béla Bartók|Béla Bartók]]'s *Concerto for Orchestra* (1943) treats the whole ensemble as soloists.

Retired Anglo-French supersonic airliner. Concorde was developed jointly by Sud Aviation and the British Aircraft Corporation under a UK–France treaty of 1962. Its first flight took place from Toulouse on March 2, 1969, and it entered service on January 21, 1976, with [[British Airways|British Airways]] and Air France. Cruising at twice the speed of sound, it halved transatlantic travel times, but [[Sonic boom|sonic booms]] restricted it to transoceanic routes. In July 2000 an Air France crash killed all 109 occupants and four people on the ground. Commercial service ended in 2003, and 18 of the 20 aircraft built are preserved.

Sexual relationship between two people who do not, or cannot, marry. Concubinage and marriage are often regarded as similar but mutually exclusive. In China until the 20th century, concubinage was an institutionalized practice that upheld concubines' rights and obligations, and concubines could be freeborn or of slave origin. The [[Code of Hammurabi|Code of Hammurabi]] records a barren wife giving her husband a slave as a concubine, whose children would be regarded as legitimate. In [[Ancient Rome|ancient Rome]], concubinatus was a monogamous alternative to marriage. After the Christianization of the Roman Empire, Christian emperors granted concubines and their children property and inheritance rights usually reserved for wives. In the 21st century some Western countries use the term as a gender-neutral legal term for cohabitation. Interpretations differ: some accounts note instances of mutual benefit, such as security for poor women, while contemporary interpretations often stress coercion and subordination.

Mild traumatic brain injury that temporarily affects brain function. A concussion results from a direct blow to the head or from forces transmitted to the head from elsewhere on the body. Symptoms may include headache, dizziness, difficulty concentrating, sleep disturbances, brief memory loss, blurred vision and mood changes, usually appearing within 72 hours. They can last two weeks in adults and four weeks in children. Common causes include motor vehicle collisions, falls, sports injuries and bicycle accidents. A [[CT scan|CT scan]] may be used to rule out severe head injuries, since routine imaging is normal after a concussion. Treatment involves relative rest for no more than one or two days, followed by gradual return to activity, and aerobic exercise may improve recovery. Worldwide, concussions affect more than 3.5 per 1,000 people a year. Repeated concussions may increase the risk of [[Chronic traumatic encephalopathy|chronic traumatic encephalopathy]], [[Parkinson's disease|Parkinson's disease]] and [[Depression (mood)|depression]].

Change of state of matter from the gas phase into the liquid phase. Condensation is the reverse of vaporization and most often refers to the [[Water cycle|water cycle]]. It is initiated by the formation of molecular clusters within a gas or at contact between a vapor and a liquid or solid surface, such as cloud condensation nuclei. It most commonly occurs when a vapor is cooled or compressed to its saturation limit. Direct transition from gas to solid is called deposition. Condensation is a crucial component of [[Distillation|distillation]], and structures such as air wells and fog fences collect water from it. Ions produced by a particle act as nucleation centers in a [[Cloud chamber|cloud chamber]], forming visible trails. Unwanted condensation in buildings can cause dampness, mold, wood rot and corrosion, and it is usually addressed by lowering indoor humidity or improving ventilation.
